title: Opinions, eh?
subtitle: Opinioni canadesi
intro: Debates at the bakery and at the Ferrante table: hockey vs soccer, Canada vs the States, whether Toronto is «really Canada», whether Chiara should learn French, and whether [[colour]] has a [[u]]. Doug, Priya, Franco and Mateo all have a view. This unit builds the B1 toolkit of opinion: modali di deduzione (must be, can't be, might be), second conditional (If I were you…), wish + past simple, connectors of contrast, and the complete map of Canadian spelling with its US and UK notes.
objectives: Fare deduzioni: [[he must be exhausted]], [[that can't be right]], [[it might rain]], [[they could be from Montréal]]
Fare ipotesi al presente: second conditional, [[If I were you, I'd learn French]], [[If I had more time, I'd read it in English]]
Esprimere desideri su un presente che non è così: [[I wish I spoke French]], [[I wish it weren't raining]]
Connettere con contrasto e sfumatura: [[however]], [[although]], [[even though]], [[on the other hand]], [[whereas]]
Scrivere colour o color, centre o center, cheque o check: ortografia canadese fra Regno Unito e Stati Uniti
canDo: B1 · Spoken production: can express and justify opinions on familiar matters with precision.
B1 · Spoken interaction: can agree and disagree politely in a lively discussion.
B1 · Writing: can write an opinion paragraph with contrast connectors and conditionals.
B1 · Reading: can follow a newspaper headline and a short opinion column, with the Canadian / US / UK spelling.
B1 · Listening: can follow a conversation where several speakers overlap and use irony.

sections.title: At the bakery, and at the Ferrantes'
sections.intro: Saturday afternoon at Doug's, then Sunday dinner at the Ferrantes'. Hockey, soccer, Toronto, Québec, and the French Chiara doesn't speak. Listen for modal deduction (must be, can't be, might be), second conditional (If I were you…) and the connectors of contrast.

blocks.title: At Doug's · the Leafs lost again
blocks.setting: Saturday 3:15 p.m., Doug's bakery on College Street. The TV above the counter is on, Toronto Maple Leafs lost 2–5 last night. Doug sweeping, Priya at the till, Mateo doing the dishes, Chiara counting pasticciotti. The customer traffic has gone.

lines.t: Five to two. Five to two! If I were the coach, I'd fire half the team. The goalie must've been asleep. You can't lose like that at home.
lines.n: Cinque a due. Cinque a due! Se fossi l'allenatore, licenzierei metà squadra. Il portiere doveva essere addormentato. Non puoi perdere così in casa.
lines.note: If I were the coach: second conditional (if + past simple + would). The goalie must've been asleep: modal deduction in the past (must have + participle, contracted must've).

lines.t: If you were the coach, there would be no team by Monday. You'd fire everyone and then you'd fire yourself. — Doug, the Leafs always lose in April. It can't be a surprise anymore.
lines.n: Se fossi tu l'allenatore, lunedì non ci sarebbe più squadra. Licenzieresti tutti e poi licenzieresti te stesso. — Doug, i Leafs perdono sempre ad aprile. Non può più essere una sorpresa.
lines.note: If you were the coach, there would be: second conditional. It can't be a surprise: modal deduction (can't be = must not be).

lines.t: I don't understand hockey. In Italy we have soccer. In Rome, there's a derby and the whole city stops. Here, the Leafs lose and the whole city goes to brunch.
lines.n: Non capisco l'hockey. In Italia abbiamo il calcio. A Roma c'è il derby e tutta la città si ferma. Qui i Leafs perdono e tutta la città va a fare il brunch.
lines.note: Soccer vs football: in Canada, soccer (as in the US). Football means the Canadian Football League, with its own rules.

lines.t: Soccer is soccer. If you ask me, hockey takes more skill. Have you ever seen a man skate backwards at 40 km/h? But I don't want to argue. On the other hand, I'd love it if the Leafs could win a Stanley Cup before I die. They haven't won one since 1967. I was eighteen.
lines.n: Il calcio è calcio. Se chiedi a me, l'hockey richiede più abilità. Hai mai visto un uomo pattinare all'indietro a 40 km/h? Ma non voglio litigare. D'altra parte, mi piacerebbe se i Leafs vincessero una Stanley Cup prima che io muoia. Non ne vincono una dal 1967. Avevo diciotto anni.
lines.note: If you ask me: fixed opinion phrase. On the other hand: connector of contrast. I'd love it if the Leafs could win: double layer: I'd love it (conditional) + if … could (second conditional).

lines.t: I agree with Chiara. Soccer is the beautiful game. Although Doug has a point about hockey, I think most Canadians know more about soccer than they admit. The World Cup is coming to Toronto in 2026. Even Doug'll watch.
lines.n: Sono d'accordo con Chiara. Il calcio è il gioco più bello. Benché Doug abbia un punto sull'hockey, credo che la maggior parte dei canadesi sappia più di calcio di quanto ammetta. La Coppa del Mondo arriva a Toronto nel 2026. Anche Doug la guarderà.
lines.note: Although Doug has a point: connector of concession. Even Doug'll watch: emphatic even. The World Cup 2026 is in Canada / US / Mexico.

lines.t: Which brings me to my real question. Chiara, be honest. Do you think Toronto is «really Canada»? Doug says no, the real Canada is west of Winnipeg. I say yes, the real Canada is here because we're half the country.
lines.n: Il che mi porta alla mia vera domanda. Chiara, sii sincera. Credi che Toronto sia «davvero Canada»? Doug dice di no, il vero Canada è a ovest di Winnipeg. Io dico sì, il vero Canada è qui perché siamo metà del paese.
lines.note: Which brings me to: a textbook connector in writing. Do you think X is «really Y»?: a classic question in a country where identity is still being written.

lines.t: If I had to vote, I'd say Toronto is Canada, obviously. But I only know Toronto. If I'd been to Winnipeg, I'd probably say something different.
lines.n: Se dovessi votare, direi che Toronto è il Canada, ovviamente. Ma conosco solo Toronto. Se fossi andata a Winnipeg, probabilmente direi qualcosa di diverso.
lines.note: If I had to vote, I'd say: second conditional. If I'd been to Winnipeg, I'd say: a mixed conditional (third + second, previewed in unit 20).

lines.t: That's a diplomatic answer, young lady. If I were you, I'd be careful before I said that in Alberta. Anyway. If you want to understand this country, you'd better learn a bit of French.
lines.n: È una risposta diplomatica, signorina. Se fossi al posto tuo, farei attenzione prima di dirlo in Alberta. Comunque. Se vuoi capire questo paese, è meglio che tu impari un po' di francese.
lines.note: If I were you: the second-conditional classic. You'd better learn: better = stronger advice, with a hint of warning.

notes.phrase: if I were the coach · if you were the coach · if I were you · if I had to vote · if you ask me
notes.note: Five second conditionals in six lines. The pattern: if + past simple + would (clean). If I were, not if I was, in careful English.

notes.phrase: the goalie must've been asleep · it can't be a surprise anymore · they could be in trouble · he might fire everyone
notes.note: Modal deduction: must (sure yes), can't (sure no), might / may / could (possible). Must've + part. = past deduction.

notes.phrase: on the other hand · although Doug has a point · which brings me to · if you ask me · to be honest
notes.note: The connectors of opinion and contrast. B1 writing needs five of them per paragraph.

blocks.title: At the Ferrantes' · colour has a u
blocks.setting: Sunday 1 p.m., dining room at Franco and Teresa's. Pasta on the table. Franco pouring wine, Teresa cutting the roast, Sofia with a laptop, Chiara at a corner with a notebook. Franco has read a Toronto Star piece on the French in Canada.
blocks.register: informal family, bilingual with heritage Italian

lines.t: I wish Chiara spoke French. If she spoke French, she could work anywhere in the country, not just here. If I were her age, I'd move to Montréal for a year.
lines.n: Vorrei che Chiara parlasse francese. Se parlasse francese, potrebbe lavorare ovunque in Canada, non solo qui. Se avessi la sua età, mi trasferirei a Montréal per un anno.
lines.note: I wish Chiara spoke French: wish + past simple = regret about the present. If she spoke, she could work: second conditional. If I were her age, I'd move: second conditional with were.

lines.t: Zio, I speak Italian and English and I'm learning the Canadian spelling of colour. One language at a time. Although I agree it would be useful. — Pass the salad, please.
lines.n: Zio, parlo italiano e inglese e sto imparando l'ortografia canadese di colour. Una lingua alla volta. Benché sia d'accordo che sarebbe utile. — Passa l'insalata, per favore.
lines.note: Although I agree it would be useful: concession + conditional. It would be useful = second conditional, apodosis only.

lines.t: He wishes everyone spoke French. He wishes the government paid more pensions. He wishes the Leafs would win a Cup. Franco's wishes have been full for forty years.
lines.n: Vorrebbe che tutti parlassero francese. Vorrebbe che il governo pagasse più pensioni. Vorrebbe che i Leafs vincessero una Coppa. I desideri di Franco sono pieni da quarant'anni.
lines.note: He wishes everyone spoke French / the Leafs would win: wish + past (for a present not-wish) / wish + would (for a future desire or complaint).

lines.t: Mum, the article Papà read was in the Star. Did you know Québec is 90% French-speaking? Montréal is bilingual, Québec City is mostly French. The sign law — Bill 101 — says every outdoor sign has to have French. If I could choose where to study, I'd go to Montréal.
lines.n: Mamma, l'articolo che papà ha letto era nello Star. Lo sapevi che il Québec parla francese per il 90%? Montréal è bilingue, Québec City è soprattutto francese. La legge sui cartelli — la Bill 101 — dice che ogni insegna all'aperto deve essere in francese. Se potessi scegliere dove studiare, andrei a Montréal.
lines.note: If I could choose, I'd go: second conditional. Facts about Québec: 90% French, Montréal bilingual, Québec City French, Bill 101 the sign law.

lines.t: Furthermore, every form from the federal government is bilingual. CBC Radio-Canada broadcasts in both. In Ottawa, public servants might lose their jobs if they can't speak both. However, in Alberta you can live a whole life without a French word. Canada is complicated.
lines.n: Inoltre, ogni modulo del governo federale è bilingue. CBC Radio-Canada trasmette in entrambe le lingue. A Ottawa, i funzionari pubblici possono perdere il lavoro se non parlano entrambe. Però, in Alberta puoi vivere tutta la vita senza una parola di francese. Il Canada è complicato.
lines.note: Furthermore: formal connector. Might lose their jobs if they can't speak: mixed modal + conditional. However: formal contrast connector.

lines.t: Can I ask something stupid? Colour has a u, centre is c-e-n-t-r-e, cheque is c-h-e-q-u-e, travelling is two l's. But I've just written favorite with no u. What's the Canadian rule?
lines.n: Posso chiedere una cosa stupida? Colour ha la u, centre si scrive c-e-n-t-r-e, cheque è c-h-e-q-u-e, travelling con due l. Ma ho appena scritto favorite senza u. Qual è la regola canadese?
lines.note: The Canadian spelling riddle. English in Canada is a mosaic of UK and US conventions, settled unevenly in the last 150 years.

lines.t: Mostly British. Colour, favour, labour, honour, neighbour: with u. Centre, metre, theatre, fibre, litre: -re. Cheque for payment, check for the rest. Programme for a theatre, program for a computer. Travelling with two l's. Realize is with z, like the Americans. If I were you, I'd use the Canadian version at work: it signals you're one of us.
lines.n: Prevalentemente britannica. Colour, favour, labour, honour, neighbour: con la u. Centre, metre, theatre, fibre, litre: -re. Cheque per il pagamento, check per il resto. Programme per uno spettacolo, program per il computer. Travelling con due l. Realize con la z, come gli americani. Se fossi al posto tuo, userei la versione canadese al lavoro: segnala che sei una di noi.
lines.note: The seven-item Canadian spelling list. Realize with -ize (like US) is standard Canadian; -ise (British) is acceptable but less common.

lines.t: And if someone writes you an email with «color» and «favorite», that person is likely American. Or they live on their phone, which spells like America. Nothing wrong with it, you just know. — Chiara, more pasta?
lines.n: E se qualcuno ti scrive un'email con «color» e «favorite», quella persona probabilmente è americana. O vive sul telefono, che scrive come l'America. Niente di male, lo sai e basta. — Chiara, altra pasta?
lines.note: If someone writes with color…, that person is likely American: first conditional (zero / first), a generalisation.

notes.phrase: I wish Chiara spoke French · I wish the Leafs would win · I wish I'd known · if only he weren't
notes.note: Wish + past simple = regret about the present. Wish + would = complaint or desire about the future. Wish + past perfect = regret about the past (unit 20). If only is the same with more drama.

notes.phrase: colour · favour · neighbour · honour · labour (UK) · centre · metre · theatre · fibre (UK) · cheque · programme (UK) · travelling (UK) · realize · analyze (US) · tire · aluminum (US)
notes.note: The Canadian mosaic: mostly British spelling of -our and -re words; mostly US for -ize, -yze and tire; a few idiosyncrasies (programme for theatre, program for computer).

notes.phrase: If I were you · if I had to vote · if she spoke French · if I could choose · if someone writes… · if they can't speak
notes.note: Second conditional (unreal present) alongside zero / first conditional (real).

notes.phrase: furthermore · however · on the other hand · although · whereas · which brings me to
notes.note: Opinion-column connectors. Furthermore adds; however and on the other hand contrast; whereas directly compares.

questions.q: In Canadian spelling, «color» and «favorite» are the standard.
questions.why: Colour and favourite with u are Canadian; without the u is American.

questions.q: «If I were you, I'd learn French» — what's the mood of «were»?
questions.why: After if, formal English keeps the subjunctive were for all persons. If I was is tolerated in casual speech.

questions.q: The goalie ___ (must + be, past deduction) exhausted. If I ___ (be) you, I ___ (fire, cond.) the coach. I ___ (wish + Leafs + win) a Cup.
questions.n: Il portiere doveva essere esausto. Se fossi te, licenzierei l'allenatore. Vorrei che i Leafs vincessero una Coppa.

sections.title: Opinions, Canada, hockey, soccer
sections.intro: Four themes: giving an opinion in English, the vocabulary of Canadian life and politics, hockey vs soccer, and the words of a debate.

ex.t: In my opinion, the Leafs will never win in April.
ex.n: Secondo me, i Leafs non vinceranno mai ad aprile.

items.note: Formal; more casual: I think, I reckon (British), I guess (US). Not use my opinion is.

ex.t: I'd say Toronto is Canada, but it's complicated.
ex.n: Direi che Toronto è il Canada, ma è complicato.

items.note: I'd say = I would say. A soft, hedged opinion.

ex.t: If you ask me, hockey takes more skill.
ex.n: Se chiedi a me, l'hockey richiede più abilità.

items.note: A classic opinion opener. Also: as far as I'm concerned.

ex.t: To be honest, I don't understand hockey.
ex.n: A essere sincera, non capisco l'hockey.

items.note: A softener: it signals you'll say what you really think. Also TBH in texting.

items.n: capisco il tuo punto, ha un senso

ex.t: I see your point, but I disagree.
ex.n: Capisco il tuo punto, ma non sono d'accordo.

items.note: Polite disagreement, acknowledges the other person first.

ex.t: You hate the cold? Fair enough.
ex.n: Odi il freddo? Ok, posso capirlo.

items.note: Very common Canadian / British agreement. US: makes sense.

ex.t: I agree with you. — I disagree.
ex.n: Sono d'accordo con te. — Non sono d'accordo.

items.note: I'm agree is wrong. I agree. Agree with + person; agree on + topic.

ex.t: Doug has a point about hockey.
ex.n: Doug ha ragione sull'hockey (su quel punto).

items.note: Partial agreement: you don't buy the whole thing but you concede one point.

ex.t: Should she learn French? — It depends.
ex.n: Dovrebbe imparare il francese? — Dipende.

items.note: It depends on + noun. The universal lubricant, in English too.

ex.t: I guess you're right. I guess so.
ex.n: Immagino di sì, hai ragione. Immagino di sì.

items.note: US-flavoured, now universal. I guess so / I guess not.

ex.t: Canada is officially bilingual: English and French.
ex.n: Il Canada è ufficialmente bilingue: inglese e francese.

items.note: Official Languages Act 1969. The federal government uses both; provinces vary.

ex.t: Québec is predominantly Francophone; Ontario is mostly Anglophone.
ex.n: Il Québec è prevalentemente francofono; l'Ontario soprattutto anglofono.

items.note: Allophone (common in Québec): a person whose first language is neither English nor French.

ex.t: Canada has ten provinces and three territories.
ex.n: Il Canada ha dieci province e tre territori.

items.note: Not states — Canadian unit is province. Provincial government ≠ federal.

ex.t: The federal government is in Ottawa.
ex.n: Il governo federale è a Ottawa.

items.note: Federal / provincial / municipal — the three levels. Each has its taxes and bureaucracy.

ex.t: The prime minister works at 24 Sussex Drive in Ottawa.
ex.n: Il primo ministro lavora al 24 Sussex Drive a Ottawa.

items.note: Not president — Canada is a constitutional monarchy. Governor General represents the Crown; the real power is the PM.

ex.t: Toronto is on the traditional territory of the Mississaugas of the Credit.
ex.n: Toronto si trova sul territorio tradizionale dei Mississaugas of the Credit.

items.note: Prefer indigenous or First Nations / Métis / Inuit to older terms. Capital I is the convention.

ex.t: Canada calls itself a mosaic, not a melting pot.
ex.n: Il Canada si definisce un mosaico, non un melting pot.

items.note: Melting pot (US): everyone blends. Mosaic (Canada): everyone keeps their shape. A deliberate contrast.

ex.t: The meeting opened with a land acknowledgement.
ex.n: La riunione si è aperta con il riconoscimento del territorio.

items.note: A short statement recognising the Indigenous land. Standard at Canadian public events.

ex.t: Canadian healthcare is public and universal.
ex.n: La sanità canadese è pubblica e universale.

items.note: Also written as two words: health care. Public, provincial (OHIP in Ontario), free at point of use. Dentistry and prescriptions mostly not covered.

ex.t: The Charter of Rights and Freedoms is in the Constitution.
ex.n: La Carta dei diritti e delle libertà è nella Costituzione.

items.note: Patriated 1982, under Trudeau père. A core civic reference.

ex.t: Hockey is on at 7 p.m. on Saturdays, religiously.
ex.n: L'hockey è in TV alle 19 il sabato, religiosamente.

items.note: In Canada, hockey means ice hockey. Field hockey is a different sport.

ex.t: The Leafs haven't won a Stanley Cup since 1967.
ex.n: I Leafs non vincono una Stanley Cup dal 1967.

items.note: Short for Toronto Maple Leafs. Verb: to cheer for the Leafs.

ex.t: The Stanley Cup is the oldest trophy in North American sports.
ex.n: La Stanley Cup è il trofeo più antico degli sport nordamericani.

items.note: Awarded since 1893. The oldest in major pro sports.

items.n: pista di pattinaggio, pista da hockey

ex.t: Every Canadian town has a rink.
ex.n: Ogni cittadina canadese ha una pista di pattinaggio.

items.note: Backyard rink: una pista fatta in cortile.

ex.t: If I were the coach, I'd fire half the team.
ex.n: Se fossi l'allenatore, licenzierei metà squadra.

items.note: Also verb: to coach = allenare. Head coach: capo allenatore.

ex.t: The goalie must've been asleep.
ex.n: Il portiere doveva essere addormentato.

items.note: Short for goalkeeper. Also used in soccer in North America.

ex.t: In Canada, soccer is popular with kids and immigrants.
ex.n: In Canada, il calcio è popolare fra i bambini e gli immigrati.

items.note: In Canada and the US, soccer. In the rest of the world, football — but Canadian football is a different game, with American-style rules.

ex.t: The 2026 World Cup has games in Toronto.
ex.n: La Coppa del Mondo 2026 ha partite a Toronto.

items.note: Jointly hosted by Canada, Mexico, and the US.

ex.t: The Leafs have the most patient fans in North America.
ex.n: I Leafs hanno i tifosi più pazienti del Nord America.

items.note: Also: supporter (soccer, more neutral). Verb: fan a team is rare — use cheer for or root for (US).

ex.t: The Leafs lost. However, their power play is improving.
ex.n: I Leafs hanno perso. Tuttavia, il power play sta migliorando.

items.note: Followed by a comma. Formal: never starts a sentence in casual texting.

ex.t: Although Doug has a point, I disagree. Even though it's late, I'll call.
ex.n: Benché Doug abbia un punto, non sono d'accordo. Benché sia tardi, chiamo.

items.note: Although / even though at the start of a clause. Though can also be at the end (I disagree, though).

ex.t: I love hockey. On the other hand, I never watch it.
ex.n: Amo l'hockey. D'altra parte, non lo guardo mai.

items.note: Pair with on the one hand (… on the other hand).

ex.t: The Habs are in Montréal, whereas the Leafs are in Toronto.
ex.n: I Habs sono a Montréal, mentre i Leafs sono a Toronto.

items.note: Direct contrast between two parallel facts. Written register.

ex.t: Furthermore, every federal form is bilingual.
ex.n: Inoltre, ogni modulo federale è bilingue.

items.note: Formal; adds. Casual: also, besides.

ex.t: I thought hockey was dangerous. In fact, soccer has more injuries.
ex.n: Pensavo che l'hockey fosse pericoloso. In effetti, il calcio ha più infortuni.

items.note: In fact = in reality (introducing a surprising / corrective fact). Infatti italiano is closer to indeed.

ex.t: Anyway, the Leafs lost.
ex.n: Comunque, i Leafs hanno perso.

items.note: Casual. Also used to change the topic. Not written as any way (= in any manner).

ex.t: I don't like hockey. Besides, I can't skate.
ex.n: Non mi piace l'hockey. Oltretutto, non so pattinare.

items.note: Adds a reason. Not the same as beside (= next to).

sections.title: Modal deduction, second conditional, wish
sections.intro: Three pieces: modal verbs for deduction (must be, can't be, might be, could be), the second conditional for unreal present (If I were you, I'd…), and wish + past simple / past perfect / would. Plus a short reference for Canadian spelling.

blocks.title: Modal verbs for deduction
blocks.rule: Modal verbs show how sure the speaker is about a fact. Three levels. Sure yes: must + base verb (you must be exhausted), must have + participle for the past (she must have been asleep). Sure no: can't + base (it can't be true), can't have + participle for the past (she can't have gone yet). Possible: might, may, could + base (it might rain, he could be right); might have, may have, could have + participle for the past (they might have missed the train). All stay the same for every person (no -s on he): she must be, he might know. Negatives: must not + base = probably not (she mustn't be home); can't + base = definitely not; might not / may not = possibly not. The contractions must've, might've, could've, can't've exist in speech but write out might have / could have. For can't have / mustn't have in writing, keep the contraction only in dialogue.

items.t: That man by the Leafs' bench must be the new coach. He can't be a player — he's wearing a tie. He might be a scout, actually.
items.n: Quell'uomo vicino alla panchina dei Leafs deve essere il nuovo allenatore. Non può essere un giocatore — porta la cravatta. Potrebbe essere uno scout, in effetti.

items.t: The Leafs' goalie must have been asleep. He can't have seen the shot. He might have been thinking about the next game.
items.n: Il portiere dei Leafs doveva essere addormentato. Non può aver visto il tiro. Forse stava pensando alla partita dopo.

items.t: Doug said «Toronto isn't really Canada». He must've been joking. — No, he was serious. He may actually believe it.
items.n: Doug ha detto «Toronto non è davvero Canada». Doveva star scherzando. — No, era serio. Potrebbe davvero crederci.

items.right: He must have been tired yesterday.

items.wrong: She don't must be at home.
items.right: She can't be at home. / She might not be at home.
items.why: Must not = probably not; can't = certainly not. No support verb.

items.wrong: They might to be from Montréal.
items.why: Modals take the base, no to.

blocks.title: Second conditional and wish
blocks.rule: The second conditional talks about unreal or imaginary present (and future) situations. Form: if + past simple, + would / could / might + base verb. The if-clause uses past simple (If I had, if I knew, if I could); the main clause uses would (or could, might) + base. With to be, careful English uses were for all persons (If I were you, if he were here). The contraction 'd is would ('d like, 'd go). Uses: (1) imaginary present (If I spoke French, I'd move to Montréal); (2) advice (If I were you, I'd learn French); (3) politeness (Would you mind if I asked a question?); (4) hypothetical choices (What would you do?). Wish + past simple: regret about the present (I wish I spoke French = sorry, I don't). Wish + would: complaint or desire for a change in another person's behaviour (I wish you'd listen; I wish it would stop raining). Wish + past perfect for past regret: full in unit 20. If only is a stronger wish, same patterns.

blocks.caption: Second conditional and wish
head: Pattern
Example
rows: If I spoke French, I'd move to Montréal.
If I were you, I'd learn French. If he were older, he'd understand.
If I could choose, I'd go to Montréal.
That would be great. I'd love to.
I wish I spoke French. I wish I had more time.
I wish you'd listen. I wish it would stop raining.

items.t: If I were the coach, I'd fire half the team. If I were you, I wouldn't fire anyone. If I had the money, I'd buy season tickets.
items.n: Se fossi l'allenatore, licenzierei metà squadra. Se fossi te, non licenzierei nessuno. Se avessi i soldi, comprerei l'abbonamento.

items.t: What would you do if you lost your job tomorrow? — I'd call my parents. Then I'd update my resume.
items.n: Cosa faresti se perdessi il lavoro domani? — Chiamerei i miei. Poi aggiornerei il curriculum.

items.t: I wish I spoke French. I wish you'd stop apologising. I wish I had more time. If only this winter were over!
items.n: Vorrei parlare francese. Vorrei che smettessi di scusarti. Vorrei avere più tempo. Se solo fosse finito questo inverno!

blocks.title: The Italian periodo ipotetico type 2
blocks.text: English second conditional = Italian periodo ipotetico della possibilità: if + past simple + would + base = se + congiuntivo imperfetto + condizionale presente. [[If I spoke French, I'd move to Montréal]] = [[se parlassi francese, mi trasferirei a Montréal]]. Were works like fossi: [[If I were you]] = [[se fossi te / al posto tuo]]. The patterns map one-to-one, except that English has only one verb form (past simple) where Italian has a special tense (congiuntivo imperfetto).

items.wrong: If I would be you, I would learn French.
items.right: If I were you, I'd learn French.
items.why: No would in the if-clause. If + past simple only.

items.wrong: If I will have money, I will buy a car.
items.right: If I had money, I'd buy a car. (unreal) OR If I have money, I'll buy a car. (first conditional, real)
items.why: Second conditional: if + past + would. Not will / will.
Wish + past simple for present regret.

items.right: I wish you would listen more.
items.why: Wish + would for a wished change in behaviour.

items.wrong: I'd learn French if I would have time.
items.right: I'd learn French if I had time.

blocks.title: Canadian spelling: colour and center
blocks.rule: Canadian English is a mix of British and American conventions. Mostly British: -our (colour, favour, honour, labour, neighbour, humour, odour, vigour); -re (centre, metre, theatre, fibre, litre, spectre, calibre); -ce vs -se noun / verb (practice noun / practise verb, licence noun / license verb — half-British; defence noun; offence noun). Mostly American: -ize / -yze endings (realize, organize, analyze, paralyze) with -ise accepted but less common in Canada; past -ed on travelled / cancelled (double l, British) but programmed (double m, mostly US now); tire (US) not tyre, aluminum (US) not aluminium, curb (US) not kerb; cheque (payment, British) but check (verify, American); programme for a theatre event, program for a computer program; grey (British) alongside gray; a few idiosyncrasies. In practice: your phone's autocorrect in Canada should be set to Canadian English; the Toronto Star and the CBC follow Canadian; a US-based employer may want US spelling.

items.t: Please favour the Canadian centre with your presence at the theatre.
items.n: Per favore onora il centro canadese con la tua presenza al teatro.

items.t: I organized the practice for the practice session — the first noun, the second verb.
items.n: Ho organizzato l'esercizio per la sessione di pratica — il primo sostantivo, il secondo verbo.

items.t: He cancelled his flight and travelled by train instead, which was cheaper.
items.n: Ha cancellato il volo e ha viaggiato in treno invece, che era più economico.

items.right: I practised the piano. (Canadian — verb) · I practiced the piano. (American)
items.why: Canadian follows British for the verb-noun split; American uses -c- for both.

items.right: I cancelled with two l's. (Canadian / British) · I canceled with one l. (American)

blocks.caption: Emphasis and contrast
head: Pattern
Example
What to do
rows: I DO like hockey. He DOES speak French.
stress do, keep the rest light
I think YES, he thinks NO.
well, I'm not sure about that.
lower pitch, slow, no stress on content
rising at the end asks for confirmation

blocks.title: Eh? — the Canadian suffix
blocks.text: The word [[eh]] has eight common uses in Canadian English. (1) Confirmation request: [[Nice day, eh?]] = don't you think? (2) Acknowledgement of information: [[He's leaving, eh?]] = oh really? (3) Opinion-marker in a story: [[We went to the lake, eh, and the car broke down]] (filler). (4) At the end of an exclamation: [[What a goal, eh!]]. (5) At the end of a direction: [[Turn left at the lights, eh?]] = you got that? (6) Statement of surprise: [[Eh? Say that again.]] = pardon? (7) Attention-check: [[Are you listening, eh?]]. (8) Instead of right? at the end of a question. Mix the eight across one conversation and nobody will know you weren't born here. — Only Canadians, Minnesotans and New Zealanders use eh with this density; UK and most of US think it's a parody.

items.t: I DO think it was a goal. The ref must've been blind.
items.n: Credo DAVVERO che fosse gol. L'arbitro doveva essere cieco.
items.note: emphatic do + modal deduction

items.t: Nice day, eh? — Not bad. Could be worse. — Oh definitely.
items.n: Bella giornata, no? — Non male. Potrebbe andare peggio. — Oh assolutamente.
items.note: eh (confirmation request) + modal + Canadian understatement

items.q: Write a six-sentence opinion paragraph defending or attacking a view about Canada or your city, using one modal deduction (must be, might be, can't be), one second conditional (If I were you…), one wish (I wish I…), one contrast connector (however, although, whereas, on the other hand) and one Canadian spelling word (colour, centre, favourite, programme, realize, travelled, defence).
items.model: In my opinion, Toronto is more Canadian than people realize. The city must be the biggest Francophone city outside Québec after Montréal — I keep meeting people on the subway who have travelled there for work and speak French every day. Although Doug says the real Canada is west of Winnipeg, I don't think that is fair. If I were him, I'd spend a weekend at a bakery in Woodbridge or at a soccer match in High Park. I wish he would stop saying it. On the other hand, I understand the Prairie point of view: the centre of the country can feel ignored. The Canadian conversation is wider than the Toronto one.
items.hint: In my opinion… · must be / might be… · Although… · If I were him, I'd… · I wish he would… · On the other hand…

sections.title: Canada vs the States, bilingualism, Indigenous Canada
sections.intro: A short map of what makes Canada not the US, the two official languages, Indigenous Canada and the mosaic.

blocks.text: Canada is not the United States

The two obvious differences are [[universal healthcare]] (every Canadian has provincial health coverage, free at the point of use, called OHIP in Ontario, RAMQ in Québec) and [[gun laws]] (owning a handgun needs a licence, serial training and a waiting period; most people never see one). Below those, several quieter ones. The country has a [[parliamentary system]] with a prime minister and a Governor General (not a president), a [[constitutional monarchy]] whose head of state is King Charles III (symbolically) and a [[Senate]] whose members are appointed. The [[Charter of Rights and Freedoms]] (1982) is the civil-rights document, not an older bill of rights. [[Metric]] is official: Canadians weigh in pounds for the person and in grams for the groceries; drive in kilometres and read Fahrenheit on the oven. [[Sorry]] is said constantly and the Apology Act 2009 made it legally not an admission of guilt. In writing, [[colour]] has a [[u]]. On the ice, [[hockey]] is a civic religion, and the Leafs' last cup was in 1967. The federal elections run on a different clock from the US. In short: close cousins, different households.

The 1969 [[Official Languages Act]] made English and French the languages of the federal state. [[Québec]] (about 23% of the population) is officially French, with [[Bill 101]] (the Charter of the French Language, 1977) requiring French on outdoor signs and in big-business workplaces. [[New Brunswick]] is officially bilingual (the only province with that status). Everywhere else, French is a minority language with small, strong communities — [[Franco-Ontarian]], [[Franco-Manitoban]], [[Fransaskois]], [[Franco-Albertan]], [[Franco-British Columbian]], the [[Acadiens]] (Maritimes) and the [[Métis]] (prairies, who speak Michif, a mix of French and Cree). On a federal form, every box has both languages. On a cereal box, every panel is both. On a cab in Montréal, [[Taxi]] (the same in both). This is why [[Chiara]] is asked whether she speaks French: in Ottawa a government job is bilingual by law, and knowing French opens half the country. Toronto, however, is 2% French; you can live well without a word of it. In Montréal, you can't — or rather, you can, but you'll miss half the city.

blocks.title: Indigenous Canada and the land acknowledgement
blocks.text: There are three constitutionally recognised Indigenous peoples in Canada: [[First Nations]] (over 600 bands, from the Mi'kmaq in the Atlantic to the Haida on the Pacific), [[Métis]] (descendants of French / Scots and First Nations communities, mostly on the Prairies), and [[Inuit]] (in Inuit Nunangat, the Arctic). Combined they are about 5% of the population. The [[residential schools]] system (from 1870 to 1996) forcibly removed Indigenous children from their families; the [[Truth and Reconciliation Commission]] (2008–2015) catalogued the harm, and 94 Calls to Action followed. The [[land acknowledgement]] (short statements like «we acknowledge the traditional territory of the Mississaugas of the Credit, the Haudenosaunee, the Anishinaabe and the Huron-Wendat») opens most public events in Canadian institutions since the 2010s. Chiara's rented basement is on the traditional territory of the [[Mississaugas of the Credit]]: the alley belongs to a longer history than the lease.

Canada's self-description — [[mosaic]], not [[melting pot]] — comes from Pierre Trudeau's 1971 multiculturalism policy and the 1988 [[Canadian Multiculturalism Act]]. The policy is: new Canadians keep their language, religion and food and still become citizens. The result: Toronto is 51% [[visible minority]] (Statistics Canada), the second-highest Punjabi-speaking city outside India, the biggest Portuguese neighbourhood west of Lisbon in Little Portugal, the largest Chinese population by metro area in North America (together with Vancouver), and Little Italy, Little Jamaica, Koreatown, Greektown, and three Chinatowns. The [[Charter of Rights and Freedoms]] (1982) is the constitutional guarantee behind all of it. The citizenship test in unit 24 covers this ground; this unit just names it so that {hero} can take part in a conversation where Doug, Priya, Franco and Mateo each hold a different piece of the Canadian story and all four are right.

groups.title: Modal deduction
rows: sure yes: must + base · must have + part. (past): the goalie must've been asleep
sure no: can't + base · can't have + part. (past): it can't be true · can't have missed
possible: might / may / could + base · might have + part. (past)
probable (expected): should + base · should have + part. (past)

groups.title: Second conditional and wish
rows: if + past simple, + would / could / might + base: if I spoke French, I'd move
were for all persons: if I were you, I'd learn French
would + base (apodosis): that would be great
wish + past: I wish I spoke French
wish + would: I wish you'd listen; I wish the Leafs would win
if only + past: if only I spoke French

rows: mostly British: -our (colour, favour, honour, labour, neighbour), -re (centre, metre, theatre, fibre, litre)
mostly American: -ize / -yze (realize, analyze), travelled kept as British double-l
noun / verb split: practice / practise, licence / license
cheque / check (payment / verify) · programme (theatre) / program (computer) · tire · aluminum · grey/gray
